guide.title: Terminal block colours: what grey, blue and green-yellow mean
guide.description: What common terminal block colours mean, from grey and blue to green-yellow ground and orange, and why your panel standard always comes first
keyTakeaways: Green-yellow is reserved for protective earth
Blue commonly marks neutral, grey or beige marks general circuits
Your customer's or shop's panel standard overrides any general convention

body.text: Terminal block colours make a panel easier to wire, check and maintain. Most manufacturers offer the same blocks in several colours, so choosing the right one is part of specifying the strip. Here are the conventions you will see most often.

head: Colour
Typical use
rows: General feed-through blocks for line, control and signal circuits
Neutral conductors; some industries also use blue for intrinsically safe circuits
Protective earth (PE) blocks that bond to the DIN rail
Circuits that can stay live from an external source when the main disconnect is off
Often used to mark DC positive and negative distribution

body.caption: Grey, blue and green-yellow versions of the same push-in block.

body.text: Green-yellow is reserved for protective earth. Ground terminal blocks in this colour are designed to make contact with the DIN rail through the mounting foot. Do not use green-yellow blocks for any other purpose, and make sure the rail itself is properly bonded.

body.caption: A green-yellow ground block connects to the rail through its foot.

body.text: A circuit fed from outside the panel, such as an interlock from another machine, may stay energized when the panel's main disconnect is open. Marking these terminals clearly, often with orange blocks or orange conductors, warns anyone working in the panel.

body.title: Your standard comes first
body.text: Colour conventions vary between standards, industries and companies. In North America, follow the electrical code, NFPA 79 or CSA requirements and the customer's specification for the job. When in doubt, follow the drawings.

Colour narrows things down, but every terminal still needs a marker. Printed markers carry the terminal or wire number from the drawings, so a technician can trace a circuit without guessing. Many shops use colour for a conductor's role and markers for its exact identity.

Jumpers, end plates and markers are often sold in several colours too. When you order coloured blocks, check whether the end plate and jumpers for that series come in the same colour or a neutral one, and put them on the same order so the strip can be finished in one go.
Colour variants are separate part numbers. When you replace a strip, list the colour of each block on your order so the replacement matches the original layout.

faqs.q: Can I use a grey block for ground?
faqs.a: No. Use a dedicated ground (PE) terminal block. It is designed to bond to the DIN rail, and its green-yellow colour identifies the protective earth for anyone working in the panel.

faqs.q: Are terminal block colours required by code?
faqs.a: Some markings are required, such as identifying protective earth. Others are conventions. The applicable code, standard and customer specification decide what is mandatory for your panel.
